chapters.title: Unit 1: Rational Numbers
chapters.description: Fractions, integers and decimals together form the rational numbers; how to represent, compare, order and operate on them.

lessons.title: Rational Numbers: Meaning, Comparing and Operations
lessons.summary: A rational number is any number that can be written as a fraction of two integers. This lesson shows how to write, place, compare and calculate with rational numbers.

sections.title: From fractions to rational numbers
sections.body:
In earlier grades you learned about **whole numbers** (0, 1, 2, 3, ...), **integers** (..., -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, ...), and **fractions**. When we put all of these together we get a bigger family of numbers called the **rational numbers**.

You already use rational numbers every day. If you share one injera equally among 4 people, each person gets **1/4**. If the temperature in Addis Ababa is 3 degrees below zero we write **-3 °C**. If a shopkeeper records a loss of 5 birr she writes **-5**. All of these are rational numbers.

sections.title: By the end of this lesson you will be able to
sections.body:
- Define a **rational number** and write one in the form a/b
- Represent rational numbers on a **number line**
- Find the **opposite** and the **absolute value** of a rational number
- **Compare and order** rational numbers using < and >
- **Add, subtract, multiply and divide** rational numbers

sections.title: What makes a number rational
sections.body:
A **rational number** is any number that can be written in the form **a/b**, where **a** and **b** are integers and **b is not zero** (b ≠ 0). Here **a** is the *numerator* and **b** is the *denominator*.

Why must b ≠ 0? Because a/b means a ÷ b, and we can never divide by zero.

Why is every integer also rational? Because any integer can be written over 1. For example 11 = 11/1 and -4 = -4/1. So every integer is a rational number, but not every rational number is an integer (for example 3/4 is not an integer).

**Opposite:** The opposite of a rational number *a* is *-a*. A number and its opposite are the same distance from 0 but on opposite sides, for example 3/5 and -3/5. Zero is its own opposite.

**Absolute value:** The **absolute value** |x| is the *distance* of x from 0 on the number line, so it is never negative. For example |-7| = 7 and |7| = 7.

**Equivalent fractions:** You can multiply or divide the top and bottom by the same non-zero number without changing the value: 1/3 = 3/9 = 9/27. Two fractions a/b and c/d are equal exactly when a × d = b × c (cross-multiplying).

sections.title: Rational numbers on a number line
sections.body: Every rational number matches exactly one point on the number line. Negative numbers sit to the **left** of 0 and positive numbers to the **right**. Notice that 3/2 (which is 1½) sits half-way between 1 and 2, while -5/2 (which is -2½) sits half-way between -2 and -3.

visual.title: Placing rational numbers
visual.caption: A is 3/2 (1½); B is -5/2 (-2½). B is smaller because it is further left.

sections.title: Worked examples
sections.body:
**Example 1 — Order from least to greatest: 3/5, -1/2, 0, 7/10.**
Step 1: Negatives are smallest, so -1/2 comes first, then 0.
Step 2: Compare 3/5 and 7/10. Make the denominators the same: 3/5 = 6/10.
Step 3: 6/10 < 7/10, so 3/5 < 7/10.
**Answer:** -1/2, 0, 3/5, 7/10.

**Example 2 — Add 3/5 + 7/10.**
Step 1: The lowest common denominator of 5 and 10 is 10.
Step 2: 3/5 = 6/10, so 6/10 + 7/10 = 13/10.
**Answer:** 13/10 (which is 1 3/10).

**Example 3 — Multiply (-2/7) × (8/11).**
Step 1: Multiply the numerators: -2 × 8 = -16.
Step 2: Multiply the denominators: 7 × 11 = 77.
**Answer:** -16/77.

**Example 4 — Divide (3/13) ÷ (2/5).**
Step 1: To divide, multiply by the reciprocal (flip the second fraction): (3/13) × (5/2).
Step 2: 3 × 5 = 15 and 13 × 2 = 26.
**Answer:** 15/26.

sections.title: Common mistakes to avoid
sections.body:
- **Thinking -5 is bigger than -1.** On the number line -5 is further left, so **-5 < -1**. With two negatives, the one with the *larger* absolute value is *smaller*.
- **Adding fractions straight across.** 1/2 + 1/3 is NOT 2/5. First make the denominators equal: 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6.
- **Forgetting to flip when dividing.** To do a ÷ b/c you multiply by c/b, not by b/c.
- **Writing a negative absolute value.** |x| is a distance, so it can never be negative.

sections.title: Memory tips
sections.body:
- **"Left is less."** On the number line, whatever is further left is the smaller number — this works for negatives too.
- **"Keep, Change, Flip"** for dividing fractions: Keep the first, Change ÷ to ×, Flip the second.
- **Same bottom to add or subtract.** You can only combine fractions once their denominators match.
- **Absolute value = how far from home (0).** Distance is always positive.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
- A **rational number** can be written as a/b with integers a and b, where b ≠ 0.
- Every integer is rational (write it over 1), but not every rational number is an integer.
- The **opposite** of a is -a; the **absolute value** |x| is its distance from 0 (never negative).
- To **compare**, place numbers on the number line — left is smaller.
- To **add/subtract**, use a common denominator; to **multiply**, go straight across; to **divide**, multiply by the reciprocal.

sections.title: Key terms
sections.body: Important vocabulary for this lesson.

glossary.definition: Any number that can be written as a/b where a and b are integers and b is not zero.
The top number of a fraction; it counts how many parts you have.
The bottom number of a fraction; it tells how many equal parts make a whole. It cannot be zero.
The number with the same size but the other sign; the opposite of a is -a.
The distance of a number from zero on the number line, written |x|; it is never negative.
Different fractions that name the same point on the number line, such as 1/2 and 2/4.
The fraction turned upside down; the reciprocal of 2/5 is 5/2.

flashcards.back: Any number you can write as a/b where a and b are integers and b ≠ 0 (for example 3/4, -2, 0.5).

flashcards.front: Why can the denominator never be zero?
flashcards.back: Because a/b means a ÷ b, and dividing by zero is undefined.
-1/8, because it is further to the right on the number line (smaller absolute value).

flashcards.front: How do you divide by a fraction?
flashcards.back: Keep, Change, Flip: multiply by the reciprocal. (3/4) ÷ (2/5) = (3/4) × (5/2).
9 — absolute value is distance from 0, so it is never negative.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a rational number?
questions.explanation: 5/0 has a denominator of zero, and division by zero is undefined, so it is not a rational number. The others can all be written as a/b with b ≠ 0.
-3/5 is further to the left on the number line than -1/5, so -3/5 is smaller: -3/5 < -1/5.
Absolute value is the distance from zero and is never negative, so |−7/2| = 7/2.
Use the common denominator 10: 3/5 = 6/10, so 6/10 + 7/10 = 13/10.
Dividing means multiplying by the reciprocal: (3/13) × (5/2) = 15/26.

questions.prompt: Which list is correctly ordered from least to greatest?
questions.explanation: Negatives come first, then 0, then 3/5 = 6/10, then 7/10. So the order is -1/2, 0, 3/5, 7/10.

chapters.title: Unit 2: Linear Equations and Inequalities
chapters.description: Finding the unknown value: solving one-variable linear equations and inequalities and showing solutions on a number line.

lessons.title: Solving Linear Equations and Inequalities
lessons.summary: A linear equation has an unknown to the first power. This lesson teaches how to solve such equations and inequalities by keeping both sides balanced.

sections.title: Finding the unknown
sections.body:
Often in life we know a result but not a starting amount. Suppose a student buys 3 exercise books and pays 45 birr in total. How much does one book cost? If we call the cost of one book **x**, then **3x = 45**. Solving this equation tells us x = 15 birr.

An **equation** says two things are equal (it has an = sign). An **inequality** says one thing is bigger or smaller than another (it uses <, >, ≤ or ≥). In this lesson we learn to solve both.

sections.title: By the end of this lesson you will be able to
sections.body:
- Recognise a **linear equation** in one variable
- Solve equations using **inverse operations** while keeping balance
- Check a solution by substituting it back
- Solve simple **linear inequalities**
- Know the special rule: **flip the inequality sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative number**

sections.title: The balance idea
sections.body:
A **linear equation in one variable** is an equation where the variable appears only to the first power, such as **2x + 3 = 11**. (There is no x² or x³.)

Think of an equation as a **balance scale**: the two sides are equal. Whatever you do to one side you must do to the other to keep it balanced. We use **inverse (opposite) operations** to get the variable alone:
- The opposite of **+** is **−**
- The opposite of **×** is **÷**

So to solve 2x + 3 = 11 we *subtract 3* from both sides, then *divide both sides by 2*.

**Inequalities** are solved the same way, with ONE extra rule: **if you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number, you must reverse the inequality sign.** For example, from -x < 2 we multiply both sides by -1 and flip the sign to get x > -2.

sections.title: Worked examples
sections.body:
**Example 1 — Solve 2x + 3 = 11.**
Step 1: Subtract 3 from both sides: 2x = 8.
Step 2: Divide both sides by 2: x = 4.
Step 3: Check: 2(4) + 3 = 11. ✓
**Answer:** x = 4.

**Example 2 — Solve 5x − 7 = 2x + 8.**
Step 1: Subtract 2x from both sides: 3x − 7 = 8.
Step 2: Add 7 to both sides: 3x = 15.
Step 3: Divide both sides by 3: x = 5.
**Answer:** x = 5.

**Example 3 — Solve the inequality 3x + 1 ≤ 10.**
Step 1: Subtract 1 from both sides: 3x ≤ 9.
Step 2: Divide both sides by 3 (positive, so keep the sign): x ≤ 3.
**Answer:** x ≤ 3.

**Example 4 — Solve -2x > 6.**
Step 1: Divide both sides by -2. Because -2 is negative, FLIP the sign: x < -3.
**Answer:** x < -3.

sections.title: Showing an inequality on a number line
sections.body: The solution x ≤ 3 means every number that is 3 or less. On a number line we shade everything to the left of 3 and include 3 itself. The point at 3 marks the boundary of the solution.

visual.title: Solution of x ≤ 3
visual.caption: B marks the boundary value 3; the solution is 3 and every number to its left.

sections.title: Common mistakes to avoid
sections.body:
- **Doing something to only one side.** If you subtract 3, you must subtract it from BOTH sides.
- **Forgetting to flip the inequality sign** when dividing or multiplying by a negative number. -2x > 6 gives x < -3, not x > -3.
- **Sign errors when moving terms.** When a term crosses the = sign its sign changes: +3 becomes -3.
- **Not checking the answer.** Always put your value back into the original equation to be sure.

sections.title: Memory tips
sections.body:
- **"Balance the scale."** Whatever you do to one side, do to the other.
- **"Undo in reverse."** To free x, undo +/− first, then ×/÷.
- **"Negative flips the sign."** Multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number reverses < to > (and ≤ to ≥).
- **"Cross the sign, change the sign."** A term that moves to the other side switches + and −.

sections.title: Practice problems
sections.body:
1. Solve x + 9 = 20. *(Answer: x = 11.)*
2. Solve 4x = 32. *(Answer: x = 8.)*
3. Solve 3x − 5 = 16. *(Answer: 3x = 21, so x = 7.)*
4. Solve the inequality -3x ≥ 12. *(Answer: divide by -3 and flip: x ≤ -4.)*

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
- A **linear equation** has the variable to the first power only.
- Keep the equation **balanced**: do the same operation to both sides.
- Use **inverse operations** to get the variable alone, then **check** by substituting.
- Solve **inequalities** the same way, but **flip the sign** when you multiply or divide by a negative number.
- Inequality solutions can be shown by **shading** a region on the number line.

sections.title: Key terms
sections.body: Important vocabulary for this lesson.

glossary.definition: A mathematical statement that two expressions are equal, shown with an = sign.
A letter such as x that stands for an unknown number.
An equation in which the variable appears only to the first power, like 2x + 3 = 11.
The operation that undoes another: subtraction undoes addition, division undoes multiplication.
A statement that one quantity is greater or smaller than another, using <, >, ≤ or ≥.
The value of the variable that makes the equation or inequality true.

flashcards.back: An equation where the variable is only to the first power, such as 2x + 3 = 11 (no x² term).
Keep it balanced: do the same operation to both sides.

flashcards.back: Subtract 3 from both sides (use the inverse operation).

flashcards.front: When do you flip an inequality sign?
flashcards.back: Whenever you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number.
Divide by -2 and flip the sign: x < -3.

questions.explanation: 2x + 3 = 11 has the variable x only to the first power and only one variable, so it is linear. The others contain x², two variables, or x in the denominator.
Subtract 7 from both sides: x = 12 − 7 = 5.
Subtract 3 to get 2x = 8, then divide by 2 to get x = 4.

questions.explanation: Subtract 2x: 3x − 7 = 8. Add 7: 3x = 15. Divide by 3: x = 5.
Divide both sides by -2 and flip the inequality sign because -2 is negative: x < -3.

questions.explanation: The equation is 3x = 45. Dividing both sides by 3 gives x = 15 birr.

chapters.title: Unit 3: Ratio, Proportion and Percentage
chapters.description: Comparing quantities with ratios, linking equal ratios as proportions, and using percentages in everyday calculations.

lessons.title: Ratio, Proportion and Percentage
lessons.summary: Ratios compare amounts, proportions set two ratios equal, and percentages express parts out of a hundred. This lesson connects all three and applies them to money.

sections.title: Comparing amounts
sections.body:
Imagine making a drink by mixing 2 cups of juice with 3 cups of water. The **ratio** of juice to water is **2 : 3**. Ratios let us compare quantities.

If a shop offers 20% off a 200 birr shirt, how much do you save and what do you pay? That is a **percentage** question. Ratios, proportions and percentages are all about comparing parts to wholes, and they appear constantly in shopping, cooking and sharing.

sections.title: By the end of this lesson you will be able to
sections.body:
- Write and simplify a **ratio**
- Recognise a **proportion** and solve for an unknown using cross-multiplication
- Convert between **fractions, decimals and percentages**
- Find a **percentage of a quantity**
- Solve everyday problems involving **discount, profit and loss** in birr

sections.title: Ratios, proportions and percent
sections.body:
A **ratio** compares two quantities of the same kind, written a : b or a/b. Like fractions, ratios can be **simplified** by dividing both parts by the same number: 10 : 15 = 2 : 3.

A **proportion** is a statement that two ratios are equal, for example **2/3 = 8/12**. Two ratios form a proportion exactly when their **cross products are equal**: a/b = c/d means a × d = b × c. This lets us find a missing value.

**Percentage** means "out of 100." The symbol is **%**. So 25% = 25/100 = 1/4 = 0.25.
- To change a **fraction or decimal to a percent**, multiply by 100: 0.4 = 40%.
- To change a **percent to a decimal**, divide by 100: 60% = 0.6.
- To find a **percent of an amount**, multiply: 20% of 200 birr = 0.20 × 200 = 40 birr.

sections.title: Worked examples
sections.body:
**Example 1 — Simplify the ratio 12 : 18.**
Step 1: The biggest number that divides both 12 and 18 is 6.
Step 2: 12 ÷ 6 = 2 and 18 ÷ 6 = 3.
**Answer:** 2 : 3.

**Example 2 — Solve the proportion 3/4 = x/20.**
Step 1: Cross-multiply: 4 × x = 3 × 20.
Step 2: 4x = 60, so x = 15.
**Answer:** x = 15.

**Example 3 — Find 20% of 200 birr.**
Step 1: Write 20% as a decimal: 0.20.
Step 2: Multiply: 0.20 × 200 = 40.
**Answer:** 40 birr.

**Example 4 — A shirt costs 200 birr with a 20% discount. What is the sale price?**
Step 1: The discount is 40 birr (from Example 3).
Step 2: Sale price = 200 − 40 = 160 birr.
**Answer:** 160 birr.

sections.title: Common mistakes to avoid
sections.body:
- **Reversing the ratio order.** The ratio of juice to water 2 : 3 is NOT the same as 3 : 2. Order matters.
- **Forgetting % means ÷ 100.** 50% of 80 is 40, not 50 × 80.
- **Cross-multiplying wrongly.** In a/b = c/d, multiply a × d and b × c, not a × c.
- **Subtracting the percent instead of the amount.** A 20% discount on 200 birr removes 40 birr, giving 160 birr — you do not subtract 20.

sections.title: Memory tips
sections.body:
- **"Per-cent = per hundred."** Always think of % as "out of 100."
- **"Of means multiply."** "20% of 200" means 0.20 × 200.
- **Cross to solve.** For a/b = c/d, draw an X: multiply across the diagonals and set them equal.
- **Simplify ratios like fractions.** Divide both parts by their common factor.

sections.title: Practice problems
sections.body:
1. Simplify the ratio 9 : 12. *(Answer: divide by 3 → 3 : 4.)*
2. Solve 5/8 = x/40. *(Answer: 8x = 200, so x = 25.)*
3. Write 3/4 as a percentage. *(Answer: 3/4 = 0.75 = 75%.)*
4. A farmer sells 50 kg of teff and 10% is set aside as seed. How many kg is that? *(Answer: 0.10 × 50 = 5 kg.)*

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
- A **ratio** a : b compares two quantities; simplify it like a fraction.
- A **proportion** sets two ratios equal; solve unknowns by **cross-multiplying** (a × d = b × c).
- A **percentage** means "out of 100"; % to decimal means ÷ 100.
- To find a **percent of an amount**, multiply.
- **Discount, profit and loss** are percentage problems: find the amount first, then add or subtract from the original price.

sections.title: Key terms
sections.body: Important vocabulary for this lesson.

glossary.definition: A comparison of two quantities of the same kind, written a : b or a/b.
A statement that two ratios are equal, such as 2/3 = 8/12.
A method for proportions: for a/b = c/d, the products a × d and b × c are equal.
A number written as a part out of 100, shown with the % sign.
An amount taken off the original price, often given as a percentage.
The amount gained when selling price is greater than cost price.

flashcards.back: A comparison of two quantities of the same kind, written a : b (for example 2 : 3).
Two ratios that are equal, such as 2/3 = 8/12; solve with cross-multiplication.

flashcards.front: How do you write 25% as a fraction and decimal?
How do you find 20% of 200 birr?
flashcards.back: Multiply: 0.20 × 200 = 40 birr.

flashcards.front: Sale price after a 20% discount on 200 birr?

Percent means out of 100, so divide by 100: 25 ÷ 100 = 0.25.
20% = 0.20, and "of" means multiply: 0.20 × 200 = 40 birr.
Cross-multiply: 4x = 3 × 20 = 60, so x = 15.

questions.explanation: The discount is 20% of 200 = 40 birr, so the sale price is 200 − 40 = 160 birr.

chapters.title: Unit 4: Data Handling
chapters.description: Collecting data with tally marks, showing it in line graphs and pie charts, and summarising it with mean, mode, median and range.

lessons.title: Collecting and Summarising Data
lessons.summary: Data is information we gather and organise. This lesson covers tally marks, line graphs, pie charts, and the four key summaries: mean, mode, median and range.

sections.title: Making sense of information
sections.body:
Suppose a teacher counts how many students come to school each day, or a shop records how many bottles of water it sells. The numbers they collect are called **data**.

Raw data is just a pile of numbers. To understand it we **organise** it (with tally marks and tables), **picture** it (with graphs), and **summarise** it (with a single typical value). This lesson shows how.

sections.title: By the end of this lesson you will be able to
sections.body:
- Collect and record data using **tally marks** and a frequency table
- Read and interpret **line graphs** and **pie charts**
- Calculate the **mean** (average) of a data set
- Find the **mode**, **median** and **range** of a data set

sections.title: Four ways to summarise data
sections.body:
**Tally marks** record counts in groups of five: four upright lines with the fifth crossing them, like a gate. This makes counting fast. A **frequency table** lists each value with how many times it appears.

Four important summaries (the first three are 'averages'):
- **Mean** = add up all the values, then divide by how many there are. It is the usual 'average'.
- **Mode** = the value that appears **most often**.
- **Median** = the **middle** value when the data is put in order. If there are two middle values, take their mean.
- **Range** = the **largest value minus the smallest value**; it shows how spread out the data is.

For example, the marks 4, 7, 7, 9, 8 (ordered: 4, 7, 7, 8, 9): mean = 35 ÷ 5 = 7; mode = 7; median = 7 (the middle one); range = 9 − 4 = 5.

sections.title: Reading a bar chart
sections.body: A chart turns numbers into a picture so we can compare at a glance. This bar chart shows how many bottles of water a kiosk sold on three days. We can quickly see Wednesday was the busiest day.

visual.title: Bottles of water sold
visual.caption: Each bar shows the number of bottles sold on that day.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body:
**The number of goals a school team scored in 5 matches was: 2, 3, 3, 5, 7. Find the mean, mode, median and range.**

Step 1 — Mean: add them: 2 + 3 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 20. Divide by 5: 20 ÷ 5 = **4**.
Step 2 — Mode: the value 3 appears twice, more than any other, so the mode is **3**.
Step 3 — Median: the data is already in order, and the middle (3rd of 5) value is **3**.
Step 4 — Range: largest − smallest = 7 − 2 = **5**.

**Answer:** mean = 4, mode = 3, median = 3, range = 5.

sections.title: Common mistakes to avoid
sections.body:
- **Forgetting to order the data before finding the median.** The median is the middle of the *ordered* list.
- **Confusing mode and mean.** Mode is the most *frequent* value; mean is the *average* you calculate.
- **Dividing by the wrong number for the mean.** Divide by how many values there are, not by the largest value.
- **Range is a single number**, not a pair. It is largest minus smallest.

sections.title: Memory tips
sections.body:
- **Mode = Most.** Both start with 'mo' — the mode is the most common value.
- **Median = Middle.** Both start with 'm' for the middle of the ordered list.
- **Mean = add then share.** Add all values, then share equally by dividing.
- **Range = Reach.** How far the data reaches: biggest minus smallest.

sections.title: Practice problems
sections.body:
Use the data set: 6, 4, 8, 6, 6.
1. Find the mean. *(Answer: (6+4+8+6+6) ÷ 5 = 30 ÷ 5 = 6.)*
2. Find the mode. *(Answer: 6, it appears three times.)*
3. Find the median. *(Answer: order to 4, 6, 6, 6, 8; the middle is 6.)*
4. Find the range. *(Answer: 8 − 4 = 4.)*

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
- **Data** is collected information; **tally marks** and frequency tables help organise it.
- **Line graphs** and **pie charts** turn data into pictures for easy comparison.
- **Mean** = total ÷ number of values.
- **Mode** = most frequent value; **Median** = middle of the ordered data.
- **Range** = largest − smallest, showing the spread.

sections.body: Important vocabulary for this lesson.

A short line used to count, grouped in fives (four lines crossed by a fifth).
How many times a particular value appears in the data.
The average: the sum of all values divided by the number of values.
The value that appears most often in a data set.
The middle value when the data is arranged in order.
The largest value minus the smallest value.

flashcards.back: Add up all the values, then divide by how many values there are.
The value that appears most often in the data.
The middle value once the data is arranged in order.

flashcards.back: Subtract the smallest value from the largest value.

questions.explanation: Total = 8 + 5 + 12 = 25, divided by 3 days = 25 ÷ 3 ≈ 8.33 bottles per day.

chapters.title: Unit 5: Geometric Figures and Measurement
chapters.description: Properties of quadrilaterals, polygons and circles, key triangle theorems, and measuring perimeter, area and volume.

lessons.title: Geometric Figures, Triangles and Measurement
lessons.summary: This lesson explores the shapes around us: quadrilaterals, polygons and circles, the angle rules for triangles, and how to measure perimeter, area and volume.

sections.title: Shapes all around us
sections.body:
Geometry is everywhere. A window is often a **rectangle**, a traditional Ethiopian **sefed** (food tray) can be a **circle**, and the roof of a **tukul** rises in **triangles**. Knowing the rules of these shapes lets us measure land, build houses and solve real problems.

In this lesson we look at the main flat shapes, an important rule about the angles of a triangle, and how to find perimeter, area and volume.

sections.title: By the end of this lesson you will be able to
sections.body:
- Name and describe **quadrilaterals**, **polygons** and **circles**
- Use the rule that the **angles of a triangle add up to 180°**
- Calculate the **perimeter** and **area** of rectangles and triangles
- Find the **circumference and area** of a circle
- Calculate the **volume** of a box (rectangular prism)

sections.title: Key shapes and formulas
sections.body:
A **polygon** is a closed flat shape with straight sides. A **quadrilateral** is a polygon with 4 sides (square, rectangle, parallelogram, etc.). A **circle** is the set of all points the same distance (the **radius**, r) from a centre.

**Triangle angle rule:** the three interior angles of any triangle always add up to **180°**. So if two angles are known, the third is 180° minus their sum.

**Perimeter** is the distance all the way around a shape (add the side lengths). **Area** is the amount of surface inside it. **Volume** is the space inside a solid.

Useful formulas:
- Rectangle: Perimeter = 2(l + w); Area = l × w.
- Triangle: Area = ½ × base × height.
- Circle: Circumference = 2 × π × r; Area = π × r² (use π ≈ 22/7 or 3.14).
- Rectangular box: Volume = length × width × height.

sections.title: A right-angled triangle
sections.body: Here is a triangle with a base of 4 units and a height of 3 units. Its area is ½ × 4 × 3 = 6 square units. The small square at corner B shows a right angle (90°).

visual.title: Triangle ABC
visual.caption: Base BC = 4, height AB = 3, so area = ½ × 4 × 3 = 6 square units.

sections.title: Worked examples
sections.body:
**Example 1 — Find the area and perimeter of a rectangle that is 8 m long and 5 m wide.**
Area = l × w = 8 × 5 = **40 m²**.
Perimeter = 2(l + w) = 2(8 + 5) = 2 × 13 = **26 m**.

**Example 2 — Two angles of a triangle are 50° and 60°. Find the third angle.**
The angles add to 180°: third angle = 180° − (50° + 60°) = 180° − 110° = **70°**.

**Example 3 — Find the area of a triangle with base 6 cm and height 4 cm.**
Area = ½ × base × height = ½ × 6 × 4 = **12 cm²**.

**Example 4 — Find the circumference of a circle with radius 7 cm (use π ≈ 22/7).**
Circumference = 2 × π × r = 2 × (22/7) × 7 = 2 × 22 = **44 cm**.

sections.title: Common mistakes to avoid
sections.body:
- **Forgetting the ½ in the triangle area.** Area of a triangle is ½ × base × height, not base × height.
- **Mixing up perimeter and area.** Perimeter is a length (around the edge); area is the surface inside (square units).
- **Using diameter instead of radius.** In area = π r², r is the radius. The diameter is twice the radius.
- **Wrong units.** Area is in square units (m², cm²) and volume is in cubic units (m³, cm³).

sections.title: Memory tips
sections.body:
- **"Triangle angles make a straight line":** 180° is a straight angle, and a triangle's angles add to 180°.
- **"Half a rectangle":** a triangle is half of a rectangle, which is why its area has the ½.
- **"Perimeter = fence, Area = grass."** A fence goes around (perimeter); grass fills the inside (area).
- **Area squared, volume cubed.** Area uses ² units, volume uses ³ units.

sections.title: Practice problems
sections.body:
1. Find the area of a rectangle 10 m by 4 m. *(Answer: 10 × 4 = 40 m².)*
2. Two angles of a triangle are 90° and 45°. Find the third. *(Answer: 180 − 135 = 45°.)*
3. Find the area of a triangle with base 8 cm and height 5 cm. *(Answer: ½ × 8 × 5 = 20 cm².)*
4. Find the volume of a box 3 m × 2 m × 4 m. *(Answer: 3 × 2 × 4 = 24 m³.)*

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
- A **polygon** is a closed shape with straight sides; a **quadrilateral** has 4 sides; a **circle** is defined by its radius.
- The **angles of any triangle add to 180°**.
- Rectangle: Area = l × w, Perimeter = 2(l + w).
- Triangle: Area = ½ × base × height.
- Circle: Circumference = 2πr, Area = πr².
- Box: Volume = length × width × height. Use **square units** for area and **cubic units** for volume.

glossary.definition: A closed flat shape made of straight line segments, such as a triangle or square.
A polygon with exactly four sides, such as a rectangle or square.
The distance from the centre of a circle to any point on the circle.
The total distance around the outside of a shape.
The amount of surface a flat shape covers, measured in square units.
The amount of space a solid occupies, measured in cubic units.
The constant ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, about 3.14 or 22/7.
